reach.rationale: The app uses zero experimental, preview, RC or canary APIs, and even its newest import (connection, stable since v15.0.0 in Oct 2024) is far outside the ~6-month recently-stable window. Everything else is long-stable App Router plumbing.

evidence: app/src/lib/api.ts:44 — the single connection() call sits inside the shared api() data-layer wrapper
app/src/lib/api.ts:30-35 — hand-rolled TTL cache replaces Next's experimental caching family in one module
containment.rationale: Nothing to contain; the only arguably-modern API is isolated in the one data-fetching module every route goes through, so a future swap (e.g. to io() under Cache Components) touches a single file.

evidence: app/src/lib/api.ts:44 — connection() is required so pages without request-time APIs are not prerendered with API data at build time (SPEC forbids build-time data)
app/src/lib/api.ts:7-9,30 — no-store fetch + 30s in-memory TTL cache honors 'data can change at any moment' without unstable_cache/use cache
app/next.config.ts:6 — turbopack.root points at app/ so Turbopack doesn't treat the repo root as the project
justification.rationale: Each modern-leaning choice buys something a stable alternative couldn't: connection() guarantees request-time data per the spec's no-prerendering rule, and the custom cache avoids the riskier unstable_cache/use cache APIs that would fight the live-data requirement.

findings.issue: connection() is the current correct stable API, but Next 16's docs state that under Cache Components it will be superseded by io(); if the team later opts into cacheComponents this call site changes semantics.
findings.suggestion: Leave as-is while not using cacheComponents; add a short note that this is the one place to revisit if Cache Components is adopted.

summary: The app is deliberately conservative: no experimental flags, no unstable_/experimental_ identifiers, and no Next 16 preview features (Cache Components, proxy.ts, Build Adapters). Its newest API, connection() from next/server, has been stable since Next 15.0.0 (Oct 2024), and every modern choice is justified by the spec's live-data/no-build-time-fetching requirements. Risk of breaking-change churn from framework upgrades is minimal.
